resources.string: LIAN finds the apps that keep working when you aren\'t using them, or quietly collect your data. LIAN itself has no trackers, no third-party code and no internet access, so nothing you check ever leaves your phone.
No trackers · no third-party code · no internet
LIAN is starting. Tap to skip.
Android itself blocks LIAN from the internet. No account, no cloud, no trackers. The proof is always one tap away in Settings.
Protection that works on its own
Turn these on once and LIAN looks out for you. You can change them anytime in Settings.
Checks every message you get, and the links in it, the moment it arrives. New apps are checked as they\'re installed.
Shows which apps keep running while you aren\'t using them.
Tells you if an app gains risky access or hides its icon.
Here\'s how your phone is doing
You\'re protected. Nothing needs you right now.

Who has too much access, and who runs when you aren\'t looking
Updates, screen lock and the settings that keep you safe
LIAN checks it on your phone
Paste a message or link and LIAN checks it right here.
Nothing here, and that\'s good news.
While Scam Shield is on, every new app is checked the moment it\'s installed.
Check an app before you install it
Got an app file (APK) from a website or a message? LIAN looks inside it in a sealed-off space. Nothing is installed.
What it would be able to access
That doesn\'t prove it\'s safe. Only open links you were expecting.

Checking new messages as they arrive
Turn it on and LIAN checks every new message for you
LIAN reads the text of message notifications to check them right here on the phone. It can\'t send anything anywhere, and it never saves your messages.
Notifications are off for LIAN, so scam alerts can\'t pop up. Warnings still appear here.
No suspicious messages so far. Warnings are kept in memory only, for 24 hours.
Earlier warnings are gone: LIAN keeps them only in memory, so they disappear after 24 hours or when the app restarts.
You copied a link. Check it?
Tip: select text in any app and tap \"Check with LIAN\", or share it to LIAN.
Paste a message; LIAN reads it and checks every link in it
No links or email addresses were found, and the text is too short to judge.
Checked on this phone. LIAN never opens links, so the sender can\'t tell you checked.
LIAN found warning signs. Don\'t enter passwords, codes or payment details on this site.
No warning signs were found, but that isn\'t proof it\'s safe. Only continue if you expected this link.
No browser is installed to open this link.
The pattern model only reads English; the wording rules still ran.
Warnings about suspicious messages and newly installed apps.
A message you just received has signs of a scam. Tap to see why before opening any link.
LIAN found warning signs in an app that was just installed. Tap to review it.

Reading the file in an isolated process…
Only install apps you were expecting, ideally from an app store. LIAN never installs anything.
What your apps can reach, and what they do when you\'re not looking
LIAN checks the apps on your phone

To find risky apps, LIAN reads the list of apps installed on this phone, and the permissions and special access each one has. This is analysed only on this phone. LIAN has no internet access, so it can\'t send this list, or anything else, anywhere.

If someone else installed it to monitor you, removing it may alert them. If you feel unsafe, save evidence first (take screenshots on another device) and consider contacting a support service before acting.
Android records when apps work in the background. Allow LIAN to read that record (Usage access). It stays on your phone; LIAN can\'t send it anywhere.
Opens the app\'s settings. Set Battery to \"Restricted\" and remove any permission it doesn\'t need.
Without usage access, LIAN shows apps that start at boot, have no battery limits or hold always-on access.
No changes found yet. Turn on Watch in Settings for a daily check.
Material You colours from your wallpaper (Android 12+).
Live evidence that LIAN can\'t use the network

Once a day LIAN re-checks your apps and settings and tells you if something important changed, such as an app gaining Accessibility access or hiding its icon. Only one-way fingerprints are stored, never the list of your apps.
Notifications are off for LIAN, so alerts can\'t reach you. Changes still appear in Apps → Changes.
Hide LIAN in screenshots and screen sharing
Stops other apps, including spyware, from capturing LIAN\'s screens.
Deletes Watch fingerprints, settings and the encryption keys. LIAN keeps nothing else.
Watch will start again from a fresh baseline.

Every result comes from hand-written rules plus two small on-device models. The rules follow published standards (Unicode, the Public Suffix List, Android\'s own security APIs). The models were trained offline from public datasets, can\'t learn on your phone, and only ever add evidence: on their own they can raise a result to \"Be careful\", never to \"Dangerous\".

None. No analytics, ads or tracking SDKs. The build fails if one is ever added (privacy gates B and C).
Only what you switch on: Scam Shield (message checks) and the daily check (Watch). Both run on the phone and can\'t send anything anywhere.
None besides an internal, signature-protected one used by Android libraries.
Unknown (for example, installed with adb or Android Studio)
Genuine: matches the published LIAN signing certificate.
Warning: this copy isn\'t signed with LIAN\'s certificate. It may have been modified.
Development build: no official signing certificate is configured yet.
App files are opened by a separate process that Android runs as isolated user %1$s, with no permissions. It just tried to read LIAN\'s own files and was refused.
Warning: the file checker is not isolated (%1$s).
Runs code instead of opening a page
This link contains script code that would run in your browser. Real websites never send links like this.
Imitates a brand with look-alike characters
Letters have been swapped for characters that look the same, such as the digit 1 for an l or letters from another alphabet. It isn\'t the real company\'s site.
This link asks Android to download or install an app. Only install apps from an app store.
Browsers ignore everything before the @ sign. The link really goes to the address after it.
The address is one or two letters away from a well-known brand\'s real address.
Brand name combined with other words
Scammers register addresses like brand-login or secure-brand. The real company doesn\'t use this address.
Brand name in front of someone else\'s address
The brand appears at the start, but the part that decides where you go is the domain at the end.
Brand name on an address it doesn\'t use
This uses a brand\'s name with an ending that isn\'t one of that brand\'s official sites.
Part of the address mixes letters from different alphabets, a common way to fake a familiar name.
Every letter comes from another alphabet but reads like an English word, a common way to impersonate a site.
The address contains characters you can\'t see, so it isn\'t what it appears to be. They are shown as ⟦U+…⟧ above.
Hidden control characters reverse part of the text, so what you read differs from the real link, for example a file ending.
The link points to a computer\'s IP address written in an unusual form to hide it.
Part of the address is encoded incorrectly, so browsers may display it differently from where it leads.
This site sells software for secretly monitoring someone else\'s phone. If someone sent it to you or it\'s in your history unexpectedly, run an app audit.
Calling or texting this number may be charged at a high rate.
Points to a file, not a website
This link refers to a file on a device. Messages rarely have a genuine reason to contain one.
The address uses encodings or unusual characters that browsers quietly convert, which makes it hard to read correctly.
The address isn\'t valid. Browsers may refuse it or handle it unpredictably.
This link carries a second address you would be sent on to. LIAN checked that one too.
This code connects to a network with no password or outdated security, so people nearby could see what you send.
Name looks like known phishing sites
LIAN\'s on-device pattern model, trained on hundreds of thousands of phishing and ordinary domains, finds this name very similar to phishing sites. On its own this is a caution, not proof.
The on-device pattern model finds this name somewhat similar to phishing sites. It counts only because other warning signs were found too.
Numeric address instead of a name
Real companies almost never send links to bare IP addresses.
LIAN never opens links, so it can\'t see where this one goes. Only open it if you trust the sender.
Ending often used by scam sites
This domain ending is cheap and often used for short-lived scam sites. On its own it isn\'t proof.
Hosted on a free website service
Anyone can create a site at this address, so it doesn\'t belong to a verified company.
Words like login, verify or refund, together with the other warnings, are typical of phishing.
The link uses http, so anything you send can be read or changed on the way.
The address names a network port that ordinary websites don\'t use.
Very long or deeply nested address
Long chains of subdomains push the real domain out of view.
This is a known domain of the company named above. Still make sure you expected the message.
No real company, government office or boss asks to be paid in gift cards. This is one of the most common scams.
Asks you to share a code
One-time codes let someone take over your accounts or approve payments. Never send a code to anyone, whoever they say they are.
Police, courts and tax offices don\'t demand urgent payment by text. Scammers use fear to rush you.
\"Hi Mum, I lost my phone\" scams ask for money soon after. Call the person on the number you already have.
Small fee for a delivery or toll
Fake \"unpaid fee\" messages steal card details. Check deliveries and tolls in the company\'s own app or website instead.
Says your account will be blocked
Threats to close or block an account unless you act now are a classic phishing pressure tactic.
Prize or reward you didn\'t enter for
Unexpected wins and rewards are used to collect personal details or fees.
Promises of guaranteed crypto profits, or requests for your wallet\'s recovery phrase, are scams.
LIAN\'s on-device pattern model, trained on thousands of real scam, spam and ordinary texts, finds this message very similar to scams. On its own this is a caution, not proof.
The on-device pattern model finds this message somewhat similar to scams. It counts only because other warning signs were found too.
Asks you to call about a charge
Scammers ask you to call \"to cancel\" a payment. Call your bank on the number on your card, not the one in the message.
Urgency is used so you don\'t stop to check. Together with the other signs it makes a scam more likely.
This matches a known product for secretly monitoring a phone: messages, location, calls. It is listed by the Echap stalkerware-indicators project.
This is a known parental-control or monitoring app. That can be legitimate, but if you didn\'t install it, someone may be watching this phone.
Pretends to be a well-known app
It uses a well-known app\'s name, but it isn\'t made by that company and didn\'t come from a reviewed store.
Has the powers banking trojans use
Accessibility combined with SMS, overlays or notification access lets an app read your screen, steal codes and act on your behalf.
It has no icon in the app drawer but holds powerful access. Hiding is typical of stalkerware.
Installed by a fake app store
The installer uses a real store\'s name but isn\'t the store that came with your phone.
Can read and control your screen
Its Accessibility service is on. It can see everything on screen and tap for you, and it doesn\'t declare itself an accessibility tool.
It declares itself an accessibility tool (like a screen reader). Make sure you switched it on yourself.
Your keyboard sees everything you type, including passwords. Use one you trust.
It can lock or wipe the phone and can be hard to uninstall.
It isn\'t your messaging app but can read SMS, including one-time codes.
It can read every notification, including messages and codes.
An app other than a store installed it, a pattern used by droppers that sneak in malware.
Built for a very old Android
Apps built for Android 5.1 or older get permissions without asking you.
Overlays can show fake login screens on top of real apps.
It\'s signed with a developer test certificate or debuggable, which real releases aren\'t.
Usage access reveals which apps you open and when.
It was installed from an APK file rather than an app store, so no store reviewed it.
It can track your location even when you\'re not using it.
It was installed over USB debugging or its source is unknown.
It\'s marked test-only, which published apps never are.
It can ask to install further apps.
It targets Android 9 or older, so newer privacy protections don\'t apply to it.
The file was changed after it was signed, or the signature is invalid. Don\'t install it.
Android won\'t install an unsigned app as is. Someone may try to get you to use a tool to install it anyway.
It only uses the old JAR signature, which is weaker against tampering.
LIAN checked the signature and that the whole file matches it.
Signed by someone else than the installed app
You already have an app with this name, signed by a different developer. Android would refuse this as an update; scammers tell people to uninstall the real app first. Don\'t.
Its name matches a well-known or installed app, but it\'s a different package from a different publisher.
Asks for the powers banking trojans use
It wants Accessibility together with SMS, overlays or notification access.
It has no launcher icon and declares monitoring services, typical of stalkerware.
It contains an Accessibility service. Only switch it on if you trust the app completely.
Will ask to be device administrator
It can ask for administrator rights, which make it hard to remove.
A keyboard sees everything you type.
A VPN app can see which sites you connect to.
Asks to read or send SMS
SMS access lets an app read one-time codes or send premium-rate texts.
It wants to read your call log or handle calls.
Asks to draw over other apps
Overlays can show fake login screens.
Android version no longer gets security fixes
Google no longer publishes security fixes for this version. Update if your phone offers it; otherwise consider a newer phone.
Android version close to end of support
This is the oldest version still getting security fixes. Update when you can.
Security patch is over 6 months old
Known security holes are fixed every month. Check for a system update.
Reported patch is newer than the hardware says
The secure hardware records an older patch than the system claims, which can mean modified system software.
Anyone holding the phone can open it, and storage encryption is weaker without a PIN or password.
Secure hardware reports the phone can run modified system software. Unless you did this yourself, treat the phone as compromised.
Secure hardware reports the system failed verification at boot.
This phone didn\'t provide a hardware attestation LIAN could verify (common on emulators and some older phones).
Google revoked a key in this phone\'s attestation chain; leaked keys are used to fake a healthy phone.
Rooted phones let apps bypass Android\'s protections. If you didn\'t root it, someone else may have.
Set a PIN or password so your data is protected by it.
Data could be read directly from the phone\'s storage.
Whoever installed them can read encrypted traffic from apps that trust them. Remove any you don\'t recognise.
A connected computer can install apps and read data. Turn it off when you\'re not developing.
Devices on the same network could connect for debugging.
They unlock settings that weaken protections. Turn them off if you don\'t need them.
Private DNS encrypts the names of sites you visit so the network can\'t read or alter them.
If a VPN is active, make sure it\'s one you chose: it can see where your traffic goes.
Android\'s strictest security mode, recommended for people at high risk of targeted attacks.
Works unseen and has no icon
It kept running in the background, yet you can\'t open it from the app drawer. Hidden apps that keep working are typical of stalkerware.
Worked unseen with access to your data
It kept running while you weren\'t using it, and it is allowed to read personal data such as your location, microphone or messages.
Can read your screen at any time
Its Accessibility service is on, so it sees everything on screen, in every app, even when you aren\'t using it.
It sees previews of all your messages and codes as they arrive.
It can track where you are even when it\'s closed.
It ran a background service while you weren\'t using it. That can be fine (music, navigation), but you should know.
Android won\'t pause it in the background to save battery.
It can launch itself in the background as soon as the phone turns on.
